profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Researcher Profile
authoring_note: Original content informed by the public framework structure and role-profile intent. No Jisc descriptor text is reproduced or closely paraphrased.

framework_structure_informed_by: Jisc BDC six-element structure and role-profile architecture
source_strategy.role_lens: Specialised profile for digitally mediated research practice across the research lifecycle.

entries.profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Researcher Profile
entries.capability_statement: In the context of a researcher managing methods, data, outputs and scholarly collaboration, keeps essential digital tasks moving but still relies on prompts, familiar routines or local help when work becomes less predictable.
observable_practices: Uses research software and devices for routine the research lifecycle when a known example or clear instructions are available.
Keeps reference and data tools moving with some structure, but consistency drops when the task becomes unfamiliar or time-pressured.
Can recover from minor issues in project files and workflows through search, help or local support, although interruptions still slow progress.
evidence_examples: Examples showing routine use of research software and devices for predictable tasks.
A simple file, checklist or message trail in reference and data tools that shows work can be completed, albeit with some friction.
A support request, self-note or reflection describing how an issue in project files and workflows was resolved.

common_misconceptions.claim: Owning or accessing many apps means the basics are secure.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Breadth of access can hide fragile workflow habits and version confusion.

common_misconceptions.claim: Getting through the task once shows the process is reliable.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: One-off success does not show independent, repeatable practice.

entries.profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Researcher Profile
entries.capability_statement: In the context of a researcher managing methods, data, outputs and scholarly collaboration, uses core tools independently, chooses sensible workflows and solves common issues without much interruption.
observable_practices: Uses research software and devices independently and chooses sensible settings or features for the job rather than relying on default habits.
Organises reference and data tools so that current materials, deadlines and permissions are easier for other people to follow.
Troubleshoots common problems in project files and workflows and makes practical choices that reduce avoidable friction.
evidence_examples: A clean, consistently used setup in research software and devices that other people can navigate without extra explanation.
A short process note, template or annotated example from reference and data tools showing independent workflow choices.
A troubleshooting example from project files and workflows where the person diagnosed and fixed a common problem.

common_misconceptions.claim: Being quick personally is the same as having a good workflow.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: A strong personal workaround may still be opaque or awkward for others.

common_misconceptions.claim: A preferred tool is automatically the right choice everywhere.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Fit depends on context, interoperability, support and inclusion.

entries.profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Researcher Profile
entries.capability_statement: In the context of a researcher managing methods, data, outputs and scholarly collaboration, optimises workflows, judges tool choices critically and improves practice for other people as well as for themselves.
observable_practices: Improves research software and devices so that reliability, accessibility or efficiency increase for a wider group, not just for personal use.
Reviews reference and data tools critically, removing duplication and simplifying the workflow where needed.
Makes well-judged decisions about project files and workflows with attention to interoperability, support burden, inclusion and risk.
evidence_examples: A redesigned or simplified approach to research software and devices adopted by others or endorsed locally.
Before-and-after evidence from reference and data tools showing improved reliability, accessibility or efficiency.
A comparison or rationale for choices in project files and workflows that weighs fit, risk, support and interoperability.

common_misconceptions.claim: Proficiency means always adopting the newest or most advanced platform.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Judgment and simplification often matter more than feature depth.

common_misconceptions.claim: If a process works for experts it should work for everyone.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Sustainable improvement must account for different users, needs and support conditions.

entries.profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Researcher Profile
entries.capability_statement: In the context of a researcher managing methods, data, outputs and scholarly collaboration, adapts existing materials or familiar methods to meet immediate needs, but design choices are still mostly guided by examples rather than by clear intent.
observable_practices: Adapts existing analysis scripts or workflows for immediate use, but most choices still follow familiar patterns rather than an explicit design rationale.
Uses digital research outputs to solve a local problem once the route is reasonably clear.
Experiments with methods prototypes or reproducible packages in a limited way, though evaluation is still mainly about whether something worked at all.
evidence_examples: An adapted version of analysis scripts or workflows based on an existing model.
A local workaround using digital research outputs that addresses an immediate need.
A brief note on what was changed in methods prototypes or reproducible packages, even if evaluation is still limited.

common_misconceptions.claim: Changing the look of something counts as innovation.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Surface polish does not by itself improve fitness for purpose.

common_misconceptions.claim: Trying a new tool is enough evidence of creative capability.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Capability lies in the problem solved and the design decisions made.

entries.profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Researcher Profile
entries.capability_statement: In the context of a researcher managing methods, data, outputs and scholarly collaboration, creates purposeful outputs or workflow changes that fit the user need, the task and the context.
observable_practices: Designs analysis scripts or workflows around the need, the users and the context rather than around the tool alone.
Uses digital research outputs to remove repeated effort or improve clarity, consistency or accessibility.
Tests and refines methods prototypes or reproducible packages enough to show that the change is genuinely useful.
evidence_examples: A purposeful design in analysis scripts or workflows with visible choices about structure, format or accessibility.
Evidence that digital research outputs reduced repeated effort or improved the user experience.
Feedback or review notes showing that methods prototypes or reproducible packages was refined after real use.

common_misconceptions.claim: A useful one-off output is automatically reusable.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Reusability usually needs documentation, testing and adaptation for others.

common_misconceptions.claim: More interactivity always means better design.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Good design serves the need; extra features can add friction.

entries.profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Researcher Profile
entries.capability_statement: In the context of a researcher managing methods, data, outputs and scholarly collaboration, designs reusable, evaluative and innovative solutions that improve practice beyond the immediate task.
observable_practices: Creates analysis scripts or workflows that other people can reuse, adapt or scale with minimal extra explanation.
Treats digital research outputs as part of an improvement cycle, with feedback and evidence informing later iterations.
Uses methods prototypes or reproducible packages to support original, well-scoped innovation rather than novelty for its own sake.
evidence_examples: A reusable package, toolkit or documented pattern built from analysis scripts or workflows.
Evidence from digital research outputs showing evaluation, iteration and decisions about scale or adaptation.
A short account of how methods prototypes or reproducible packages changed practice beyond the immediate task.

common_misconceptions.claim: Innovation means large-scale disruption every time.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Many proficient innovations are focused, evidence-led and appropriately scoped.

common_misconceptions.claim: Once a digital solution works, evaluation can stop.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Proficient practice keeps learning from use, context change and feedback.

entries.profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Researcher Profile
entries.capability_statement: In the context of a researcher managing methods, data, outputs and scholarly collaboration, learns reactively when a new need appears and often stops once the immediate task is complete.
observable_practices: Uses methods training when a new need arises, but development activity is still mostly reactive and short-term.
Tries out ideas from research practice experiments in isolated moments without always checking what changed in practice.
Joins scholarly peer learning when prompted or when confidence is low, though follow-through may be limited once the pressure passes.
evidence_examples: Completion of methods training linked to an immediate need.
A brief example of trying something from research practice experiments once or twice in practice.
Participation records or notes from scholarly peer learning with limited follow-through.

common_misconceptions.claim: Watching training content is the same as improving practice.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Development is visible only when learning is applied and reflected on.

common_misconceptions.claim: Only formal courses count as digital development.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Practice, peer exchange and experimentation also matter.

entries.capability_statement: In the context of a researcher managing methods, data, outputs and scholarly collaboration, plans and applies digital development in a way that strengthens real practice over time.

Uses research practice experiments to build confidence through application, reflection and adjustment.
Contributes to scholarly peer learning in a way that both supports personal growth and helps keep knowledge current.
evidence_examples: A development plan or reflection that links methods training to a concrete change in practice.
Evidence from research practice experiments showing experimentation, review and adjustment over time.
Contributions to scholarly peer learning that show reciprocal learning rather than passive attendance.

common_misconceptions.claim: Confidence grows just by repeating the same task.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Confidence deepens when practice is challenged, reflected on and adapted.

common_misconceptions.claim: Personal development is enough even in collaborative settings.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Some digital change depends on shared language, routines and support.

entries.capability_statement: In the context of a researcher managing methods, data, outputs and scholarly collaboration, creates conditions for shared digital learning, reflection and confidence building in others as well as in self.
observable_practices: Curates or shapes methods training so that development becomes easier and more coherent for others.
Uses research practice experiments to make practice visible, reflective and evidence-informed at group level.
Builds scholarly peer learning that support confidence, transfer and sustained change rather than one-off exposure.

Facilitated use of research practice experiments with evidence that confidence or practice shifted across a group.
A sustained contribution to scholarly peer learning that strengthens ongoing development culture.

common_misconceptions.claim: Helping others learn means simply sharing favourite tips.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Enabling growth requires structure, empathy, follow-up and adaptation.

common_misconceptions.claim: Attendance proves that development has happened.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Proficient development looks for transfer into real practice.

entries.profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Researcher Profile
entries.capability_statement: In the context of a researcher managing methods, data, outputs and scholarly collaboration, finds usable sources or data for immediate tasks, but evaluation of quality, limitations and relevance is still inconsistent.
observable_practices: Uses literature and data searches to locate material for immediate tasks, but source quality checks are still inconsistent.
Reads datasets or codebooks with some care, though assumptions, gaps or definitions can still be missed.
Draws on evidence syntheses to support decisions, but confidence is sometimes based more on convenience than on evidence strength.
evidence_examples: A saved set of literature and data searches used to complete an immediate task.
A worked example using datasets or codebooks with some attention to meaning, though not all assumptions are checked.
A note or draft using evidence syntheses that shows a plausible but still limited evidence base.

common_misconceptions.claim: A source is reliable if it appears high in search results or looks professional.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Presentation and ranking do not guarantee trustworthiness or fit.

common_misconceptions.claim: Numbers speak for themselves.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Data always depends on definitions, omissions, context and interpretation.

entries.profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Researcher Profile
entries.capability_statement: In the context of a researcher managing methods, data, outputs and scholarly collaboration, judges source quality, data definitions and relevance deliberately, then uses evidence with care.
observable_practices: Uses literature and data searches deliberately to compare relevance, credibility and fit for purpose.
Interprets datasets or codebooks with attention to definitions, missing information, timeframe and context.
Uses evidence syntheses to make reasoned judgments and can explain the limits of the evidence.
evidence_examples: An evidence trail from literature and data searches showing source comparison and selection criteria.
An annotated interpretation of datasets or codebooks that explains caveats, definitions or missing data.
A decision note using evidence syntheses that distinguishes stronger from weaker evidence.

common_misconceptions.claim: Rejecting biased sources is the same as critical literacy.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Critical literacy often requires weighing imperfect evidence, not just discarding it.

common_misconceptions.claim: A neat dashboard is automatically decision-ready.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Visual clarity can conceal weak measures, missing data or poor alignment with the question.

Interrogates datasets or codebooks critically and explains uncertainty, bias or methodological limits to other people.
Turns evidence syntheses into decision-ready insight while making confidence levels and open questions visible.

A briefing on datasets or codebooks that makes uncertainty, bias or method limitations visible to others.
A decision-ready summary from evidence syntheses with confidence statements and clear open questions.

common_misconceptions.claim: Evidence work is objective if the analyst stays neutral.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Judgments still need transparency about methods, assumptions and limits.

Contributes in research communities or networks when expectations are clear, though collaboration can become messy when several channels compete.
Joins public engagement channels as a participant, but does not yet consistently shape how others can engage.

Examples from research communities or networks showing participation, though updates or decisions may be hard to track.
Visible engagement in public engagement channels as a contributor rather than a facilitator.

common_misconceptions.claim: Using many channels improves communication.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: More channels can create duplication, confusion and exclusion.

common_misconceptions.claim: Fast responses are the main sign of good digital collaboration.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Purpose, clarity and inclusivity often matter more than speed alone.

entries.profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Researcher Profile
entries.capability_statement: In the context of a researcher managing methods, data, outputs and scholarly collaboration, chooses channels and collaboration methods intentionally to support the task, the audience and inclusive participation.
observable_practices: Chooses co-authoring and project spaces to match audience, task and timing rather than using the same pattern for everything.
Organises research communities or networks so that updates, decisions and contributions are easier to follow.
Uses public engagement channels in ways that support respectful, inclusive and purposeful participation.
evidence_examples: A clear channel plan or working agreement for co-authoring and project spaces.
Examples from research communities or networks showing concise updates, accessible records and purposeful coordination.
Evidence that public engagement channels enabled useful participation from more than one kind of contributor.

common_misconceptions.claim: A lively chat space guarantees collaboration.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: High activity may still produce weak decisions, poor records or uneven participation.

common_misconceptions.claim: Formal tone always makes communication more professional.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Professional communication also needs openness, accessibility and fit for purpose.

context_dependencies.role: This profile assumes the respondent is operating in the specialist role context of Researcher; use adjacent profiles only as contextual references.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Interpret examples and acceptable evidence in light of discipline norms; the standard of capability stays the same but the tools, genres and risk points may differ sharply by subject area.
context_dependencies.institution_type: Institution type affects priorities, support models and examples, but the underlying progression remains comparable.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Institution level matters where research roles span doctoral study, research staff and principal investigator responsibilities.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Digital confidence should not be confused with capability; look for reliable practice and judgment, not just fluent self-presentation.

prerequisites: Stable developing-level practice in routine tasks.
Opportunities to apply digital choices independently in real work or study.
cross_element_dependencies: Progress is easier when Digital Proficiency and Productivity is at least emerging alongside this element.
Progress is easier when Digital Learning and Development is at least emerging alongside this element.
Progress is easier when Digital Identity and Wellbeing is at least emerging alongside this element.
entries.respondent_visibility: Visible to collaborators, learners, service users or community members who experience the communication pattern.
progression_signals: Facilitates collaboration rather than only contributing to it.
Participation becomes more balanced and inclusive.

entries.profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Researcher Profile
entries.capability_statement: In the context of a researcher managing methods, data, outputs and scholarly collaboration, facilitates productive collaboration or community participation and shapes better digital communication norms.
observable_practices: Designs or facilitates co-authoring and project spaces so that collaboration is clearer, more balanced and more resilient.
Uses research communities or networks to support collective decision-making, accountability and participation across different needs.
Shapes public engagement channels by modelling good norms, managing tension early and helping others contribute well.
evidence_examples: A facilitated structure for co-authoring and project spaces that improved collaboration quality or inclusion.
Records from research communities or networks showing balanced participation, decision clarity and follow-through.
Examples from public engagement channels where norms were shaped deliberately and conflict or exclusion was handled well.

common_misconceptions.claim: Facilitation means posting most often.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Good facilitators create space for others and guide participation deliberately.

common_misconceptions.claim: If conflict is visible, collaboration has failed.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Handled well, tension can improve clarity and decision quality.

entries.profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Researcher Profile
entries.capability_statement: In the context of a researcher managing methods, data, outputs and scholarly collaboration, responds to digital identity or wellbeing issues after they arise, with actions that are often platform-specific or temporary.
observable_practices: Adjusts researcher profiles and identifiers after an issue appears, though the response is often temporary or limited to one platform.
Manages reputation and openness choices inconsistently, leading to cycles of overload, distraction or blurred boundaries.
Responds to workload and wellbeing practices when prompted, but does not yet maintain a deliberate long-term approach.
evidence_examples: A reactive change to researcher profiles and identifiers after a concern or incident.
Short-term use of reputation and openness choices to reduce overload or distraction.
A note or reflection about workload and wellbeing practices that identifies a risk but has not yet become a stable practice.

common_misconceptions.claim: Changing one privacy setting solves digital identity risk.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Presence, boundaries and context usually span several platforms and practices.

common_misconceptions.claim: Overload is just a personal time-management issue.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Digital environments and expectations also shape attention and wellbeing.

entries.profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Researcher Profile
entries.capability_statement: In the context of a researcher managing methods, data, outputs and scholarly collaboration, manages presence, privacy, boundaries and digital habits deliberately across contexts.
observable_practices: Reviews researcher profiles and identifiers deliberately so that public traces, privacy and role expectations are better aligned.
Uses reputation and openness choices to support sustainable work patterns, healthier boundaries and appropriate availability.
Treats workload and wellbeing practices as an ongoing part of trustworthy participation rather than a one-off compliance task.
evidence_examples: A deliberate review of researcher profiles and identifiers with role-appropriate choices about visibility, privacy or tone.
A sustained routine in reputation and openness choices that supports healthier availability and attention.
Evidence that workload and wellbeing practices is being managed as an ongoing practice rather than as a one-off fix.

common_misconceptions.claim: Good privacy settings are enough to manage digital identity.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Tone, boundaries, visibility, reputation and role expectations matter too.

common_misconceptions.claim: Wellbeing is separate from digital practice.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Availability, platform habits and communication norms affect wellbeing directly.

entries.profile_name: Jisc Building Digital Capability Researcher Profile
entries.capability_statement: In the context of a researcher managing methods, data, outputs and scholarly collaboration, models and shapes healthy, trustworthy and context-aware digital norms for wider groups or communities.
observable_practices: Uses researcher profiles and identifiers to model clear, context-aware digital presence for other people.
Shapes reputation and openness choices in ways that support care, inclusion and sustainable participation beyond personal habits alone.
Contributes to workload and wellbeing practices by helping groups think well about trust, boundaries, risk and wellbeing.
evidence_examples: Shared guidance or modelling related to researcher profiles and identifiers that other people use or reference.
Group norms or a support approach using reputation and openness choices to improve sustainable participation.
A reflective or advisory piece about workload and wellbeing practices that helps others balance trust, care and risk.

common_misconceptions.claim: Role modelling means telling others to follow the rules.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Proficient practice shapes culture through care, explanation and context-sensitive guidance.

common_misconceptions.claim: The safest digital presence is minimal visibility everywhere.
common_misconceptions.why_inaccurate: Healthy identity management balances opportunity, trust and risk rather than disappearing.
